notes.meaning: About fifty-seven years after the temple was finished, a new leader named Ezra stepped forward during the reign of King Artaxerxes. The text traces his family tree through famous priests like Hilkiah and Zadok back to Seraiah, the high priest killed when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem. In Bible lists, calling someone a 'son' often means a grandson or later descendant. This long family line proves that Ezra had true priestly authority.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern historians suggest Ezra may have journeyed to Jerusalem later under Artaxerxes II around 398 BC, rather than under Artaxerxes I in 458 BC.

notes.meaning: The family record continues all the way back through Phinehas and Eleazar to Aaron, the first high priest of Israel. Ezra skips a few generations here to keep the list brief, focusing on the most important figures. Tracing his lineage to Aaron shows the Jewish people that Ezra was fully qualified by birth to serve God at the altar.

Ezra traveled from the Jewish community in Babylon to Jerusalem. He was a skilled scribe, meaning he was not just a penman who copied scrolls, but a doctor and trusted teacher of the Law of Moses. The Persian king gave Ezra everything he asked for because the Lord's favor and blessing rested on him.

A second large group of exiles left Babylon with Ezra in the king's seventh year, around 458 BC. This company included ordinary Israelites along with priests, Levites, temple singers, gatekeepers, and temple helpers. Each group had a specific role in restoring regular worship at the house of God in Jerusalem.

The travelers left Babylon on New Year's Day in the first month and reached Jerusalem on the first day of the fifth month. Their nine-hundred-mile trip took four full months because families with small children, elderly relatives, and supplies had to move at a gentle pace. Ezra credited their safe arrival entirely to God's gracious hand protecting and guiding them.

Ezra dedicated his whole life to three clear goals: studying God's Word, obeying it in daily life, and teaching its rules to Israel. He understood that a leader must first know the truth and practice it personally before trying to guide others. God's favor was on Ezra because his heart was devoted to honoring Scripture.

King Artaxerxes issued a formal written decree giving Ezra official imperial backing. The king addressed Ezra with great respect as both a priest and an expert scholar in the Lord's commandments. This royal letter guaranteed Ezra the authority he needed to carry out his mission.

The letter opens in Aramaic, the official language used for government business across the Persian Empire. Artaxerxes uses his imperial title, 'king of kings,' which meant he ruled over many smaller nations and local kings. He sends a warm greeting of peace to Ezra, recognizing him as an honored scholar of the God of heaven.

The royal decree announced that any Israelites living in the Persian Empire could freely choose to go to Jerusalem with Ezra. No one was forced to leave their homes, but the door was wide open for those who longed to return. This gave priests, Levites, and ordinary people complete freedom to go back to the land of promise.

The king and his seven closest royal advisers sent Ezra on an official fact-finding mission. He was ordered to examine conditions in Judah and Jerusalem to see if the people were living in obedience to God's law. Ezra carried a copy of the Scriptures in his hands as the standard for his evaluation.

Artaxerxes and his counselors contributed a generous gift of silver and gold to honor the God of Israel. Ezra was also authorized to gather freewill gifts from Persian subjects across Babylon and from fellow Jews who chose to stay behind. All these voluntary gifts were set apart specifically to support the temple in Jerusalem.

The king ordered that this collected money be spent right away on bulls, rams, and lambs, along with the grain and drink offerings that went with them. After buying the sacrifices, Ezra and the other leaders were given total freedom to spend the remaining funds as seemed best according to God's will. The pagan king trusted Ezra's honesty so deeply that he gave him full discretion over the royal treasure.

The king also gave Ezra precious vessels to be used for sacred duties inside the temple. These were newly donated ceremonial dishes given as gifts of goodwill by the Persian court. Ezra was instructed to deliver every single one of them directly to God's house without holding anything back.

If any other supplies or repairs were needed for the temple, Ezra was permitted to draw money directly from the royal treasury. This gave him access to imperial government funds whenever unexpected expenses came up. God used a foreign empire's wealth to ensure His house was properly maintained.

Artaxerxes sent a strict command to all the Persian governors and treasurers west of the Euphrates River to give Ezra whatever supplies he requested without delay. The king set generous maximum limits: tons of silver, hundreds of bushels of wheat, and large amounts of wine and olive oil. He placed no limit at all on salt, ensuring that the priests would never run out of what was required for sacrifices.

The king insisted that everything commanded by the God of heaven be carried out with great care. Like many rulers of his time, Artaxerxes feared that neglecting a local god might bring divine anger down upon his empire and his sons. God used the king's dread of judgment to provide safety and resources for His worship.

The royal decree banned tax collectors from demanding any tribute, toll, or duty from anyone who served at the temple. This special tax break protected priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, and temple helpers alike. Being free from heavy taxes allowed these workers to focus entirely on leading God's people in worship.

Ezra was granted authority to appoint judges and magistrates across the province to enforce God's law among the Jewish people. Along with establishing a fair legal system, he was instructed to teach God's commands to anyone who had never learned them. The decree combined civil justice with religious education so that the whole community could know and keep the truth.

Anyone who refused to obey God's law and the king's royal decree was to be judged quickly and firmly. The appointed courts were given power to punish offenders through execution, exile, fines, or prison. The Persian government backed God's commandments with full legal force to keep peace and order in the land.

After quoting the royal decree, Ezra pauses to praise the Lord, the God of his ancestors. He knew that the king's generous desire to honor the temple did not come from human goodness, but because God had placed that desire into the king's heart. Whenever rulers do good things for God's people, the praise belongs entirely to the Lord.

Ezra thanked God for extending loyal covenant love to him before the king, his counselors, and all the empire's powerful princes. Knowing that God's strong hand of favor was with him filled Ezra with bold courage to lead. He was then able to gather leading men from Israel to return with him to Jerusalem.
